I have always wondered why ordinary mornings feel like minor miracles. Before the world wakes, the kettle clicks, pale light gathers along the kitchen window, and the house seems to hold its breath. Then someone yawns, a chair scrapes, and reality begins.

We spend much of our lives arranging small responsibilities into shapes we can understand. Calendars become rivers, priorities become maps, and unanswered messages drift downstream like leaves. Yet the best moments rarely arrive according to plan. They appear in borrowed jackets, familiar jokes, warm bread, or the sudden realization that someone was listening all along.

I think creativity resembles gardening more than construction. A gardener cannot command rain, but she can prepare soil, choose seeds, and wait. She removes weeds without resenting them for being weeds. Sometimes growth is dramatic; sometimes it is barely visible. Still, she returns each morning because attention itself is a form of faith.

Perhaps this is why I write. Not to capture life perfectly, but to notice it more closely. A sentence can preserve the particular blue of evening light, the awkward silence after a confession, or the feeling of standing at a train station with no clear destination. Words need not freeze a moment; they can remind us that moments continue, quietly, beyond the page.

Today, I will leave room for surprise. I will drink the tea while it is hot, answer a postponed message, and walk without optimizing the route. Perhaps I will find a street, a cat, or a song.
